on.verdict: Rex lobs the baseball at 8.47 m/s. It reaches Ollie 1.24 s later at 8.47 m/s. It hits his waiting hands with 68.3 N to 171 N, and his arms bring it in over 91 cm. One round trip takes about 4.05 s (the throws and flights).
status: Gentle lob: 8.47 m/sHis arms then stop it: a sliver of his strengthHis stop goes to the endless ocean: their power
tiles: Throw8.47 m/s46° up · gentle lobFlight1.24 stop 4.62 mArrives at8.47 m/s46° downHits his palms with68.3 N to 171 Nfirst contact, over in 7.2 ms to 18 ms · 48 g or more on the baseballOllie slidesnothinghis stop goes to the endless ocean: their powerRound tripabout 4.05 sthrows and flights
effort: All-out: no cap needed. Nothing the lab checks in this test can do harm here (nearest people and buildings 5 m away), so they go all-out.Courtesy ceiling: none. Nothing in this test does harm, even all-out, with the nearest people and buildings 5 m away. They take their own recoil: the thrower’s push back and the catcher’s stop go to the endless ocean, so nothing in this test pushes on the ground to shake it.
happens: Catching is stopping momentum, and here most of it happens in the first instant. His hands wait at full reach, and with his forearms they weigh 132 kg, more than the baseball. When it hits them they move off together, and nearly all of its energy goes into squashing his palms and the baseball by about 3 cm to 7.6 cm (an estimate). That’s the 68.3 N to 171 N, and the catch itself is over in about 7.2 ms to 18 ms. Bringing it in to his chest (91 cm) takes as long as he likes: he has strength to spare, and the gentlest steady push that does it, 1.03 N, takes 3.27 min.Air resistance absorbed: their power takes back all of the air’s drag on it, so it flies drag-free: no slowing, no heating and no boom from its flight.They take their own recoil: the push back from the throw (1.2 kg·m/s) goes into their source, the endless ocean, so none of it reaches the ground.They take their own recoil: stopping it is Ollie’s own push, so its push back (1.2 kg·m/s, the baseball’s momentum) goes into their source, the endless ocean, and none of it reaches the ground.The round trip counts the throws and the flights. With strength to spare, each catcher brings the baseball in to his chest as slowly as he likes, so that part has no set time.
Stopping it puts 6.14 J (1.5 mg TNT) into his palms and arms. It ends up as heat in his indestructible plush.
math: Aim: the gentlest throw is the angle needing the least launch speed, each speed solved so the arc comes down at Ollie’s hand height (2.74 m) where his hands meet it, 1.82 m in front of his centre. Same air and round-Earth model as Throw. Fastball: his full-strength speed at each angle; the flattest angle whose path passes Ollie’s hands. Catch: first contact with his hands (m_h = 132 kg): v₁ = v m/(m + m_h); energy lost ½ m m_h v²/(m + m_h), over a 3 cm–7.6 cm squash (1–2.5% of his height, an estimate). Then his feet hold (They take their own recoil: he is planted): F = (m + m_h) v₁²/(2d) + m g sin(angle), up to the most his arms can push; if that isn’t enough, it reaches his chest at v² = v₁² − 2d(F − m g sin(angle))/(m + m_h). d = 0.3 × his height = 91 cm. First contact lasts about 2 × squash / v. At the arm force F the stroke takes t = (v₁ − v)/a (v = 0 where his arms stop it), a = (F − m g sin(angle))/(m + m_h); at the least force that works, t = 2d/v₁. The round trip counts that stroke only when it is forced (his arms can’t stop it, or need at least half his strength); otherwise he can take as long as he likes.
